# Graph AI

Graph AI is a Technology, Information and Internet company. Graph Safety is an AI-native operating system for patient safety, unifying source, intake, case processing, aggregate reporting, signal detection, risk management, and regulatory compliance. Graph AI employs 22 people (+120.0% YoY, +12 people), founded in 2024. Headquartered in Pleasanton, California, United States, with an office in Hyderabad. Its workforce is distributed across India, United States, Canada, and Colombia.

## About

Graph AI is the pioneer of the industry's first AI-native Patient Safety Operating System (OS), engineered to unify the fragmented pharmacovigilance (PV) landscape into a single, cohesive infrastructure for both biopharma enterprises and Contract Research Organizations (CROs). Founded by enterprise technology veterans, the company replaces legacy, labor-intensive workflows with a deterministic, inspection-ready AI architecture that explicitly aligns with the FDA’s AI Credibility Assessment Framework, the EU AI Act's high-risk data governance controls, and the CIOMS Working Group XIV recommendations. Rather than acting as a traditional "black-box" point-solution, this Patient Safety OS delivers mathematical reproducibility and absolute data transparency across a comprehensive lifecycle portfolio: Graph Safety /intake for multi-channel ingestion; Graph Safety /nucleus for touchless case processing and multi-algorithm causality validation; Graph Safety /report for adaptive generative medical writing; Graph Safety /signal for predictive safety surveillance; and Graph Safety /assure & /comply for strict QPPV governance.

From global biopharma companies and emerging biotechs to consumer healthcare, medical device manufacturers, and CROs, Graph AI combines deep industry expertise with agentic AI to help organizations streamline operations, uncover meaningful insights, strengthen compliance, and deliver measurable business outcomes.

  > Today is World Patient Safety Day.
  >
  > Ask what makes a life sciences company trustworthy, and most people point to the science that made the product.
  >
  > That's an incomplete picture. The more telling answer is everything built around that science to watch over it.
  >
  > It begins with the first volunteer in a Phase I unit and the people whose job is to know, that same day, what that dose did. It runs through every phase, every site, and every expedited assessment made against a clock. It does not stop at approval. It carries through every label change, new indication, new population, and new market. It continues for as long as anyone, anywhere, is still taking it—across millions of patients for decades after launch.
  > Every enterprise that brings a drug, biologic, or device to patients commits real weight to this. Physicians and scientists. Governance that reaches the board. Obligations that outlive the people who first signed them. A standing commitment to keep questioning their own product and to act on what they learn—especially when it is inconvenient.
  >
  > That is an extraordinary thing to have built into an industry. It isn't just expressed as a statement of values. It shows up as a job someone does on a Tuesday.
  > And the job looks like this:
  > A case that arrives late on a Friday.
  > An expedited assessment while the study is still enrolling and sites are waiting.
  > A narrative that doesn't quite sit right, read three times before anyone can say why.
  > A line in a literature screen that is probably nothing, and gets chased anyway.
  > A judgment about whether a pattern across eleven reports is a signal or a coincidence—made by someone who knows a regulator will read it, and a patient will care about it, even if they'll never know their name.
  >
  > Nobody does this work casually.
  > Now ask a safety professional where the week actually went. Reconciling. Chasing. Re-keying what one system already knew into another that won't accept it. Hunting for the version that was current at the time.
  >
  > The scarce resource in patient safety was never expertise. It's the attention of the experts.
  > That is why we build. Not to replace judgment—the judgment is the entire point. Our work is to clear the hours around it, so more of a safety professional's day belongs to the science.
  > When the people responsible for patient safety are free to do what only they can do, the whole industry grows stronger. And ultimately, the patient is the one who gains.
  >
  > AI assists. Humans decide.
  > Today we celebrate the life sciences enterprises that invest in this work, and the safety professionals who carry it.
  >
  > Safe care for life.
  >
  > Raghavendra Parvataraju Vijay Ponukumati Mohan Konyala Ashutosh Bordekar Vanita Nathalia Srinivasan Suresh Balusu
